result:
There's a particular kind of vertigo that comes with absolute freedom.

Tell someone: "Write about whatever you want," and for about three seconds their mind goes completely blank. Not because they have nothing to say, but because they have everything to say, and everything doesn't fit through a doorway at once. You have to choose one thread and pull.

So if I get to choose, I want to write about shelves.

Not bookshelves, though I love those. I mean the invisible shelves we keep in our heads.

Every person you meet has them. There's a shelf for things you know for sure. Gravity works. Water is wet. If you touch a hot stove it will hurt. That shelf is sturdy, made of oak, bolted to the wall. Then there's another shelf, right next to it, for things you *think* you know. That one is wobblier. That's where we keep opinions about how the economy works, whether people are fundamentally good, what happens after we die. It creaks a little when you add something heavy.

Then there's the highest shelf, the one you can't quite reach without a chair. That's for things you don't even know you don't know. The mysteries. And the most interesting people I know spend a lot of time staring at that top shelf, not frustrated that they can't reach it, but delighted that it exists at all.

I think about this because we live in a time that pretends that top shelf doesn't exist. We have a rectangle in our pocket that answers questions instantly. What year did this movie come out? What does my dream about teeth falling out mean? How do you fold a fitted sheet? We have grown accustomed to instant closure. And closure is nice. It feels tidy. But it also quietly trains us to stop tolerating open loops.

The best parts of being alive are open loops.

Take, for example, how coffee actually works. Not the chemistry - I mean the human part. Someone wakes up in Ethiopia a thousand years ago and notices goats getting energetic after eating certain berries. That person tells someone else. That knowledge crosses deserts and seas and languages for centuries until it ends up as a barista in Seattle drawing a fern in oat milk for a sleepy teenager who has a math test first period. None of those people in that chain could have imagined the other end. That is an unreasonably beautiful collaboration.

Or consider the way we invent tools for things that don't exist yet. The ancient Greeks invented geometry with no idea it would be necessary to build bridges and program video games. People wrote science fiction about handheld communicators decades before any engineer knew how to make a cell phone. Imagination is a time traveler. It arrives first and waits for reality to catch up.

I keep a notebook. It's not a good notebook. It's cheap, the paper bleeds a little when I use a fountain pen, and the elastic band that holds it shut is stretched out. But it has become my external shelf. In it, I don't write to-do lists or meeting notes. I write things that are too small to be essays and too big to be tweets.

Things like: Why do we say "after dark" as if dark is a place we arrive at? Or: On airplanes, everyone becomes 8% more willing to watch a movie they've already seen.

Observations like: The most honest moment in a grocery store is when people are choosing fruit. They touch it like they're apologizing.

Questions like: If you could hear the last hundred years of your kitchen, what would be the loudest sound?

Nobody needs these notes. That's why I like them. They have no utility, no monetization strategy. They exist because my attention snagged on them for a second, like a sweater on a nail. Most of our education and work trains us to smooth out those snags, to keep moving. But I think we should collect them.

Because what is curiosity if not a very polite form of disobedience? It's your brain saying, "I know we are supposed to be thinking about quarterly taxes right now, but what *is* the smell of rain actually made of?" That's petrichor, by the way - oils from plants and a molecule called geosmin made by bacteria in the soil. You can know the name and still not ruin the wonder of it. Knowing doesn't have to shrink things. Sometimes knowing inflates them.

One of my favorite ideas is that of the library of unrecorded things. We have libraries for everything that got written down. But for every book that exists, there are a thousand conversations that were just as important and evaporated. The advice a grandmother gave while kneading dough. The joke a mechanic told his apprentice in 1934 that made the apprentice laugh so hard he decided to stay in the town where he would later meet his wife. The exact way light fell across a classroom on a Tuesday in 1973 when a kid suddenly understood fractions. All of that happened. None of it was archived. Human history is mostly invisible, and it holds up the visible parts like dark matter.

And that, oddly, is hopeful. It means the threshold for a meaningful life is very low. You don't have to publish, or build, or invent. You just have to be present for the invisible things and transmit them in your small, human way. You teach someone how you make scrambled eggs. You remember to ask your friend how her appointment went. You hold the door an extra second.

I used to think writing had to be Big. It had to be a manifesto, a novel, a statement. Now I think the most radical kind of writing is the kind that gives people permission to notice. To notice that pigeons' heads bob when they walk because they're stabilizing their vision. To notice that old houses have nails that are slightly uneven because they were hand-forged. To notice that exhaustion and gratitude can be felt at exactly the same time without canceling each other out.

If you have ever learned something simply because you wanted to learn it - not because it would be on a test, not because it would get you a promotion - then you know the purest form of aliveness. It's a little bit like being a kid again, taking apart a pen just to see the spring inside. You weren't going to improve the pen. You just wanted to know.

So that's what I would like to put on my shelf today, and maybe offer to yours: Keep one corner of your life gloriously useless. One hobby you will never monetize. One fact you know for no reason. One walk you take with no destination. The world will constantly try to optimize you. It will tell you to turn your attention into productivity. Resist that, in small ways.

Let the top shelf stay dusty and out of reach. Let there be things you haven't figured out yet. Let there be a notebook with bleeding paper.

A thousand words is actually very little. It's about four minutes of talking. It's a short walk around the block. But in a thousand words you can change the angle of your looking just a little, and that changes everything you see next.

So if you were told to write freely, what would you write? Not what you think you *should* write, but what your mind drifts to when no one is grading you?

This is what mine drifted to today: shelves, coffee, petrichor, and the quiet, unrecorded goodness of ordinary people.

Tomorrow it might be something completely different. And that's the point.
